title: Where the limiter sits: one check before any expensive work
caption: The gateway asks the shared counter store before forwarding. Rejected requests never reach the API servers or the database.

steps.text: A request arrives at the edge, tagged with its key (user id, API key or IP).
The limiter atomically increments the key's counter in a fast shared store and reads the result: one round trip, about 1 ms.
Under the limit: forward. The API servers and database only ever see allowed traffic.
Over the limit: answer 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After right away. The rejection costs almost nothing.

scenarios.name: Over the limit
scenarios.summary: The 11th request in a window of 10: rejected at the edge, so the API and database never see it.

steps.text: Request 11 of this minute arrives for the same API key.
INCR returns 11, which is above the limit of 10.
Reject now: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After: 23 (seconds until the window resets).
Nothing behind the limiter is touched: that's the whole point of rejecting early.

scenarios.name: Counter store down
scenarios.summary: The limiter can't reach its counters. You must decide in advance: fail open (serve, unprotected) or fail closed (reject everyone).

steps.text: INCR times out: the counter store is down or partitioned away.
Fail open (most public APIs): forward the request and page someone. Users are fine; the API is briefly unprotected.
Fail closed (login, OTP, payments): return 429/503. Abuse stays blocked, but so does everyone else.

scenarios.name: Alternative: in each service
scenarios.summary: No central gateway: every service limits with a local token bucket. One less hop, but each instance only sees its own traffic.

steps.text: The load balancer spreads one user's requests across both instances.
Each instance checks its own in-memory bucket: no network hop, about 1 µs.
Catch: with N instances a user can get up to N × limit. Set each bucket to limit ÷ N, and accept that the limit is approximate.

scenarios.name: Risk: retry storm
scenarios.summary: Clients that retry 429s immediately multiply the load. The limiter survives, but the counter store and the network take the hit.

steps.text: Badly written clients retry at once, in a tight loop: 10× the traffic, every request still hitting the counter store.
Mitigation: send Retry-After, have SDKs back off with jitter, and block repeat offenders at the CDN/edge before they reach the limiter.
